clue.text: King has not returned from dance

parts.note: Charles is the name of several English kings

indicators.note: returned says the little word not is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

explanation.surface: A king who refuses to come back from a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns NOT into TON, which follows CHARLES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Charleston is a lively 1920s jazz-age step.

explanation.surface: Repairing something with a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: To cobble is to repair shoes or patch together; a cobble is also a rounded paving stone.

clue.text: Great displeasure in the Stock Exchange recently ?

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Fury on the trading floor over the latest market moves.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across the join of 'Exchange' and 'recently'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger is strong displeasure, a synonym.

clue.text: Painter needed in the crow's nest, perhaps

definitions.text: needed in the crow's nest, perhaps

explanation.surface: An artist sent up the mast of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits as LAND SEER: one who sights land, the lookout's job in the crow's nest, the platform high on a ship's mast.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edwin Landseer was a Victorian animal painter; a lookout aloft watches for the shore.

indicators.note: going wrong says the letters of the little word was are scrambled

parts.note: RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Someone who once was green has gone off the rails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going wrong' turns WAS into SWA; 'way' then gives RD. 'Green' looks like an adjective about inexperience but means a stretch of turf.
explanation.definitionFit: A sward is an expanse of short grass, like a village green.

clue.text: Regulation formerly made about drain repair

indicators.note: about says one piece is wrapped around another here

parts.note: once means formerly, at an earlier time

indicators.note: repair says the letters of drain are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: An old rule about fixing the drains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repair' turns DRAIN into RDINA, and 'about' sets ONCE around it: O(RDINA)NCE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an official rule or decree, a by-law.

parts.note: unreturnable tennis serves are what the first sense means, and cutting a pack of cards can turn up the top cards of each suit

explanation.surface: Public services facing budget cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Services' reads as public provision, but these are tennis serves no one returns, and the cards one hopes to cut to.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis an unreturned winning serve is called by the same name as the highest card in each suit.

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
a table is a list of figures or items

explanation.surface: A painter pores over a list.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable was the English landscape painter of The Hay Wain.

clue.text: Promising to make notes about clothes

indicators.note: about says the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: to sing is to make musical notes
wear means clothes, as in evening wear

explanation.surface: Someone vowing to jot down remarks on fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make notes' suggests writing, but these are musical notes; SING goes round WEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing is vowing or giving a solemn promise.

parts.note: taken as written
the Fal is a river in Cornwall

explanation.surface: The useless stretches of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The FAL is a river in Cornwall, in south-west England, flowing out at Falmouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is waste or refuse, literally the bits that fall off when a carcass is butchered.

parts.note: de is the French and Spanish word for of
a fence is a criminal who receives stolen goods

explanation.surface: A case clearing a foreign offender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of foreign' asks for 'of' in a foreign language: French DE. A FENCE is a crook who handles stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A defence is a justification or vindication of a person or action.

explanation.surface: A home and the plot it stands on.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Lords is Parliament's upper chamber; Lord's is the London cricket ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Peers sit in the upper parliamentary chamber, and the famous cricket venue in St John's Wood carries the same name.

parts.note: a don is a fellow of a university college
a caster is one who casts a line, an angler

explanation.surface: Another fisherman met up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow-angler' reads as one companion, but splits into DON (a college fellow) and CASTER. DONCASTER is a town in South Yorkshire, in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is a place lying within that northern English county, a railway and racing town.

parts.note: under means short of, as in under the limit
a ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A junior employee has run out of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An underling is a person of lower rank, a subordinate.

clue.text: But old enough for a stripe as well as a star

definitions.text: But old enough for a stripe as well as a star

parts.words: But old enough for a stripe as well as a star
parts.note: every US state has a star on the American flag, but only the thirteen original colonies are also counted in its stripes; the opening words contrast a name meaning recent with a long history

explanation.surface: Something both young and old earns two flag emblems.
explanation.walkthrough: The state's name begins with a word meaning recent, yet it was one of the thirteen original colonies, so it is honoured by a stripe on the flag as well as a star; a jersey can also be striped.
explanation.definitionFit: This US state was one of the thirteen founding colonies represented by the flag's stripes, besides having its own star.

parts.note: a land is a country
a grave is an accent mark slanting down over a letter

explanation.surface: Is a rural twang worth counting?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a verb but is a noble title; the GRAVE accent is the mark in à.
explanation.definitionFit: A landgrave was a German count holding jurisdiction over a territory.

clue.text: Some job, anchoring in this port !

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A ship's task of dropping anchor in a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: OBAN is a port on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Oban is a ferry harbour town in Argyll, Scotland.

explanation.surface: A remark destined for fame.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe is to remark, and also to keep or mark a festival.

parts.note: cool means indifferent or unenthusiastic

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of Gide are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A head of state reads a French author's book without enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: André Gide was a French novelist; 'novel' looks like his book but signals that GIDE becomes IDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin Coolidge was the thirtieth US president.

explanation.surface: Assuming control of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bowler takes an over: six deliveries in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer delivers an over by bowling; a bowl is also a round dish.

parts.note: an ant lives in an anthill
to elope is to run away to marry

explanation.surface: A mountain inhabitant flees from the beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hill-dweller' suggests a mountain goat but means an insect of the anthill.
explanation.definitionFit: Antelopes are hoofed grazing mammals such as gazelles.

clue.text: Discuss right to put in complaint

indicators.note: to put in says one letter goes inside the other piece

parts.note: an ague is a fever, an old word for an illness or complaint

explanation.surface: Debating the right to lodge a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complaint' reads as a grievance but means an illness, AGUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To argue is to debate or discuss a point.

indicators.note: upset in a down clue says the word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a sop is a small concession made to pacify someone
set means firm, as a jelly sets

explanation.surface: A company is annoyed by a bar licence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns SOP into POS.
explanation.definitionFit: A posset is a hot drink of milk curdled with ale or wine.

clue.text: Eight go round the old transport plant

indicators.note: go round says the first piece encircles what follows

parts.note: taken as written
ye is an old form of the
BR is British Rail, the former national railway

explanation.surface: A rowing eight carries an old boat around the factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory but is a flower. BR is British Rail, Britain's former national rail network.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyebright is a small wild flower once used to treat eye ailments.

explanation.surface: Craving another smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's novel the orphan Oliver Twist famously asks for more gruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's orphan asked for a second helping; twist is also tobacco spun into a rope.

clue.text: Is the member with nothing on consigned here and forgotten ?

parts.note: a limb is a member of the body
O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A naked club member has been shelved and forgotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with nothing on' reads as naked but places O after LIMB.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put in limbo is left neglected in a state of oblivion.

clue.text: It was eaten with a runcible spoon

definitions.text: It was eaten with a runcible spoon

parts.words: It was eaten with a runcible spoon
parts.note: Edward Lear's poem The Owl and the Pussy-cat has the couple dine on a chopped meat dish and slices of quince with this nonsense spoon

explanation.surface: Recalling what was eaten at a nonsense-verse wedding feast.
explanation.walkthrough: The runcible spoon is Lear's invented utensil; the line is 'They dined on mince, and slices of quince'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's verse names finely chopped meat as the dish the owl and cat ate with the spoon.

clue.text: Vaults are distributed round one river

are distributed says the letters of vaults are spread out into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'are distributed' turns VAULTS into VSTULA, which goes 'round' I: VI STULA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vistula is Poland's longest river, flowing through Warsaw.

explanation.surface: Scoring a tally of official orders.
explanation.definitionFit: To indent is to notch an edge; indents are also official orders for goods.

clue.text: Weekly contributors are in bewilderment, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word is judged by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a daze is a state of bewilderment

explanation.surface: Columnists for a weekly paper are all confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weekly contributors' suggests journalists; the seven units that make up a week are meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Each week is made up of seven of these units of time, so they contribute to it.

clue.text: Community of Yorkshire people meet Test opener

parts.note: Settle is a market town in North Yorkshire
men means people

indicators.note: opener picks the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Yorkshire cricket folk meet the opening batsman of a Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: SETTLE is a small town in North Yorkshire, northern England. 'Test opener' suggests a batsman but gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: A settlement is a small community, such as a village.
